{"text":"EMERGENCY – Come straight down! 🚑"}
{"text":"Signs of Heat Stroke"}
{"text":"Excessive panting, drooling, weakness, collapse, vomiting, diarrhea, seizures."}
{"text":"Immediate First Aid"}
{"text":"Remove from heat source immediately."}
{"text":"Apply cool (NOT ice-cold) water to body and fan."}
{"text":"Transport to clinic immediately."}
{"text":"Heat stroke is life-threatening and requires emergency treatment."}
{"text":"Description"}
{"text":"Urgency"}
{"text":"RED OR ORANGE: Assess severity — determine if the pet is having an allergic reaction!"}
{"text":"Procedure"}
{"text":"Book with any vet — general appointment duration."}
{"text":"If the patient has swelling, vomiting/diarrhoea, or can't breathe, they must come down immediately — possible anaphylactic reaction!"}
{"text":"For Your Information"}

{"text":"Pet can be showing signs of pain and irritation eg licking or chewing at the area bitten, or limping/not weight bearing. The bite is usually in an area with little hair eg foot pads, belly or face/nose."}

{"text":"If the pet is showing signs of discomfort only or localised pain at the bite site (none of the serious symptoms above), we should still see the pet. The vet may choose to give an anti-histamine injection or pain relief to make the animal more comfortable."}
{"text":"If the Owner Can't or Won't Come In"}

{"text":"Owner can apply a cold compress (wrapped in a light tea towel) to the bite for up to 10 minutes and monitor the pet at home over the next 24 hours. They may also put the limb into a cold water foot bath if the foot was bitten."}
{"text":"It is important the client watches the pet for 24 hours. They must come down immediately or go to the Emergency Centre (if after hours) if any of these signs develop:"}
{"text":"Swelling on face."}
{"text":"Vomiting & diarrhoea."}
{"text":"Description"}
{"text":"Pet is not interested in eating at all or will only eat small amounts. Their eating habits have changed. Pet may also be lethargic or showing no interest in activity."}
{"text":"Urgency"}
{"text":"Urgent — assess urgency by asking appropriate questions."}
{"text":"Procedure"}
{"text":"Book with any vet — general appointment duration."}
{"text":"Book an early appointment where possible in case further workup is required eg blood tests."}
{"text":"For Your Learning"}
{"text":"Loss of appetite in pets is a common symptom. The cause can be as simple as a mild stomach upset, but it could also be a sign of serious disease."}
{"text":"Common reasons for pets to be off their food:"}
{"text":"Dental issues."}
{"text":"Pain."}
{"text":"Nausea."}
{"text":"Stress."}
{"text":"Adverse reaction to drugs."}
{"text":"Internal obstructions."}
{"text":"Changes in the environment."}
{"text":"Kidney failure."}
{"text":"Pancreatitis."}
{"text":"Cancer."}
{"text":"Gastroenteritis."}
{"text":"Infection."}
{"text":"Questions to Ask"}
{"text":"How long has the pet been off food?"}
{"text":"Is the pet vomiting or having diarrhoea?"}
{"text":"Has the pet experienced weight loss?"}
{"text":"Does the pet have any underlying medical conditions?"}
{"text":"Description"}
{"text":"Vomiting: Most commonly a reaction to a minor stomach upset but can be a sign of something serious."}
{"text":"Diarrhoea: Caused by a variety of factors, including dietary indiscretion, food allergies or sensitivities, infections, parasites, and certain medical conditions."}
{"text":"Urgency"}
{"text":"RED OR ORANGE: Assess severity."}
{"text":"Procedure"}
{"text":"Book with any vet — general appointment duration."}
{"text":"Vomiting should be seen as early as possible in case the patient needs working up."}
{"text":"When Is It Urgent?"}
{"text":"Blood in the vomit — must be seen straight away."}
{"text":"Bloody diarrhoea — must be seen straight away."}
{"text":"Heatstroke — if the animal is overheating and vomiting, this is a medical emergency."}
{"text":"Advice to Clients"}
{"text":"If diarrhoea is present — ask the client to bring in a sample if possible (clean plastic container or glass jar with lid). No need to refrigerate."}
{"text":"Some Causes (Not a Full List)"}
{"text":"Ate too much."}
{"text":"Ate too fast — regurgitation straight after eating."}
{"text":"Ate grass."}
{"text":"Diet change or food intolerance."}
{"text":"Viral infections."}
{"text":"Motion sickness."}
{"text":"Heatstroke."}
{"text":"Swallowed something toxic."}
{"text":"Sign of serious illness eg pancreatitis, liver issues, constipation, parvo, urine infection, kidney issues."}
{"text":"Possible Treatments"}
{"text":"Strongly depends on the cause of vomiting, but may include:"}
{"text":"Medication and sent home."}
{"text":"Admitted to hospital for further workup which may include blood tests, X-rays or ultrasound."}

VACCINATION CAT



VACCINATION CAT


Description

  • Vaccination is to protect against viruses, some of which are fatal.

Urgency

  • NOT URGENT - next available appointment

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Procedure

  • Book with preferred vet - appointment times below
  • Book appointments on the hour eg 8am, 9am, 10am (where possible)

For each pet

  • 20min appt – Full health exam + vaccination plus ONE issue
  • 30min appt – Full health exam + vaccination plus TWO issues (charge extended appt)

{"text":"Read the Following to the Client After Booking"}
{"text":"Now that we have the appointment made, I'm going to send you an SMS with a link to all of the information you'll need to prepare for surgery."}

{"text":"Continue with their usual feeding routine. It is important that food NOT be withheld prior to admission as small animals have a higher metabolic rate than cats or dogs so fasting may cause gastrointestinal complications. Due to this, we also need you to pack them a lunch including their favourite food, so we can offer this to them during recovery."}

{"text":"There will also be information on after-care, like caring for stitches (if required) & when you need to come back & see us. It will also go through the potential risks & complications for an anaesthetic for birds & small animals. You should receive that text any moment with the link."}
{"text":"If you have any further questions, give us a call and we'd be happy to help you again."}
{"text":"Make sure the mobile number is correct and send the SMS before you hang up!"}
{"text":"Making an Appointment — Birds, Guinea Pigs, Rats & Mice"}

{"text":"All patients must have been seen by one of our vets PRIOR to making a surgical booking. If they have not been seen before, make a consultation time at least 1 day prior to the procedure date."}
{"text":"1. Check client file to ensure mobile number is correct (or make up a client file)."}
{"text":"2. Ensure you book the procedure on a day that we have an Exotic Vet on — not all vets can perform exotic surgery."}
{"text":"3. Book into correct column eg General surgery, Xrays etc."}
{"text":"4. When making appointment, ensure the Admit Time is first followed by the procedure eg \"8.10am admit — Rat lump removal\"."}
{"text":"5. Be clear about the booking — don't just write \"Lump removal\". Is it a Guinea Pig? Is it a rat? Is it a bird? BE CLEAR!"}
{"text":"Admission times: 8.00am–9.00am — allocated 10 minutes."}
{"text":"Important Notes"}
{"text":"Do NOT withhold food for birds, guinea pigs, rats & mice prior to surgery."}
{"text":"NOT URGENT — Routine procedure performed under anaesthetic."}
{"text":"Advice to Clients"}

{"text":"\"It's important I don't miss anything with regards to booking the groom, so I'm going to read out some information from the checklist that I have. This will make sure we book the procedure perfectly\"."}
{"text":"Food & Water"}
{"text":"No food after 10pm the night before the groom."}
{"text":"No water after 8am the morning of the procedure. Your cat can drink overnight."}
{"text":"Admission Time"}
{"text":"Surgical admission times start at 8am and take around 5–10 minutes."}
{"text":"I will send you an SMS with a link to a video that will go over everything you need to know prior to your cat coming in. Please make sure you watch the video."}
{"text":"Send the client the text message now!"}
{"text":"For Your Information"}

{"text":"There are various reasons why cats may need to be shaved, but the most common reasons are to remove matted hair, and to help keep cats cool during warmer weather. Cats with long coats should be brushed daily, but some cats don't tolerate brushing very well and make the process near impossible for their loving owners."}

{"text":"It's also difficult for long haired cats to regulate their body temperature on hot, humid days, so keeping their hair nice and short will help prevent them from overheating. Some cats have an extreme fear, or anxiety response to grooming procedures and will react with biting and scratching. This can lead to stress-induced health issues. To keep both your cat & our nurse safe, we only groom cats under anaesthetic."}

{"text":"While the groom itself is routine, there is no such thing as a routine anaesthetic or an easy anaesthetic. Putting an animal under anaesthetic is never without risk, so it's important for us to follow our usual procedures to ensure your cat will be as safe as possible while under anaesthetic."}

{"text":"A pre-anaesthetic blood test is compulsory for all cats over the age of 8 years. At the age of 8, cats are classed as Geriatric, and older animals can experience age-related changes in their organ function."}

{"text":"Impaired organ function can affect how the body processes and eliminates anaesthetic drugs, potentially increasing the risk of complications. By identifying potential health concerns before an anaesthetic is given, vets and pet owners can make informed decisions about whether to proceed."}

{"text":"If you are a new client and your cat has not been seen by one of our veterinarians, a consultation will be required prior to admission. We can book this in on the morning of your cat's groom. For existing clients, a consultation is not required if your cat has had a physical exam in the past 12 months and received a clean bill of health. For cats with underlying medical conditions, we must have seen your cat within the past 6 months."}

{"text":"Please make sure they have not had anything to eat after 10pm the night before the groom. It is safe for a cat to continue to drink overnight, but remove the water bowl in the morning when you wake up."}
{"text":"Groom Choices"}
{"text":"Long mane or short mane"}
{"text":"Boots or socks"}
{"text":"Lion tail or full tail"}
{"text":"When your cat goes home, please ensure they are kept inside until the following morning. Your cat is able to eat and drink as normal when you go home."}
{"text":"Appointment Panel Notes"}
{"text":"Existing VL client? YES — consultation required if not seen in 12 months (healthy cats) or 6 months (underlying conditions). Advise there may be a consultation fee."}
{"text":"Existing VL client? NO — must have a consultation booked at admission. Advise there will be a consultation fee."}
{"text":"Cat 8 years or older? Pre-anaesthetic blood test is compulsory."}
{"text":"If consultation required: book in surgical column AND in a vet's column at the same admit time eg \"8.20 Vet Admit — Cat Clip — New Client\"."}
{"text":"Make sure you send the text with the cat video! It goes through all pre & post op info & what to expect. Cat Clip SMS: https://rb.gy/pdxax"}
{"text":"About Progress Exams"}
{"text":"Progress exams are follow-up consultations to assess healing and recovery after surgical procedures."}
{"text":"Timing Guidelines"}
{"text":"Desexing: 10-14 days post-op for suture removal"}
{"text":"Dental procedures: 7-10 days post-op"}
{"text":"Orthopaedic surgery: 14 days post-op, then 6-8 weeks"}
{"text":"Soft tissue surgery: 10-14 days for suture removal"}
{"text":"Trauma repair: As recommended by vet"}
{"text":"What to Check During Progress Exam"}
{"text":"Incision healing and any signs of infection"}
{"text":"Swelling or discharge"}
{"text":"Patient's pain level and comfort"}
{"text":"Movement and activity level"}
{"text":"Removal of sutures or staples if appropriate"}
{"text":"Booking Progress Exams"}
{"text":"Schedule at time of initial surgery booking"}
{"text":"Can be a nurse appointment (vet approval required)"}
{"text":"Allow 15 minutes for consultation"}
{"text":"Post-Operative Instructions"}
{"text":"Provide written discharge instructions at surgery"}
{"text":"Remind clients to follow restricted activity guidelines"}
{"text":"Advise on wound care and monitoring"}
{"text":"Provide contact details for after-hours concerns"}

{"html":"

ATE A FOREIGN OBJECT🚑 


Description

One of the more common and potentially life-threatening conditions seen in veterinary practice is foreign body obstruction.

 

Procedure

 

URGENT - Come straight down

"}

{"html":"

For your information

 

Common items ingested/eaten are;

 

  • Tissues
  • Articles of clothing (especially underwear & socks),
  • Sticks & rocks
  • Food wrappers
  • Bones
  • Children's toys
  • Condoms
  • Hair ties (cats)
  • Other foreign objects
  •  

It is likely that the patient will need bloodwork, X-rays or even surgery, so you want to admit the patient as early in the day as possible. Nurses will triage the patient of a vet is not available. Inform them the pet is coming down.

 

If the pet ate the silly object within the last 2 hours, we will make them vomit (if safe) and hopefully they vomit the object back up. If they don't, or its too late to induce vomiting


"}

{"html":"

For the Client


Time is critical! 🚑

An intestinal or stomach obstruction can compromise or cut off the blood supply to vital tissues. If this happens the tissue may die or be irreparable

"}

{"html":"

Whelping Dogs (Giving Birth)


AN URGENT CONSULTATION IS REQUIRED FOR ANY BIRTHING DIFFICULTIES 

 

Procedure

 

  • Urgent appointment - come straight down


"}

{"html":"



"}

{"html":"

For your learning

 

Signs of GDV

 

  • Non-productive regurgitation, or attempting to vomit
  • Appearing bloated / distended abdomen
  • Drooling
  • Restlessness
  • Panting
  • Collapse

 

  • Bloat in dogs becomes life-threatening when it becomes Gastric Dilation-Volvulus (GDV). Bloat GDV happens when a dog’s stomach has rotated or twisted. Large and deep chested dogs are most at risk.
  • Certain breeds are pre-disposed to GDV. They are Great Danes, St. Bernards, Weimaraners, Irish Setters, Standard Poodles, and Doberman Pinschers.
  • It often occurs after the dog has just eaten.
  • During desexing, we can perform a Gastropexy to avoid GDV. During a Gastropexy, we will surgically 'tack' the stomach to the right side of the body wall. This will hold the stomach in place, preventing it from twisting which results in GDV. 


"}

{"html":"

TRUE EMERGENCY DOGS CAN DIE IN 1-2 HOURS

"}

{"html":"

{"html":"

FELINE LOWER URINARY TRACT DISEASE (FLUTD) 🚑


Description

 

  • Feline lower urinary tract disease (FLUTD) is a term that refers to several conditions affecting a cat’s lower urinary tract, including the urethra (a thin tube that carries urine) and bladder. 
  •  

Urgency

 

  • EMERGENCY – Come straight down! 🚑

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Procedure

 

  • Book with any vet - general appointment duration


"}

{"html":"

If treatment is not given within 24-48hrs of becoming blocked, the cat can die.

"}

{"html":"

For your learning

 

  • A male cat which is not urinating freely, requires immediate veterinary attention, because a life-threatening urinary blockage may be present.
  • Owners often confuse a blocked bladder with a constipated cat as they see the cat straining in the tray, so assume it’s to poo.
  • The cat may also be licking at their privates a lot.
  • If a client says ‘My cat is constipated’ explain to them it’s most likely the cat can’t pee (if it’s male) & they need to come down immediately. If treatment is not given within 24-48hrs of the cat becoming blocked, it can certainly die.
  • The blockage causes acute kidney failure. 


"}

{"html":"

CHOCOLATE TOXICITY 🚑


Description

Dogs are unable to metabolize theobromine (the main toxin found in chocolate). Humans can metabolize theobromine but it’s toxic to dogs. The darker the chocolate, the more toxic it is.

 

​​​​​​​Procedure

EMERGENCY – Come straight down! 🚑 

 

"}

{"html":"

Advice to clients​​​​​​​ 👈

 

Ask the client to bring down the chocolate wrapper. It will help us calculate approximately how much theobromine the pet has ingested.

Ask the client to bring down the chocolate wrapper.

"}

{"html":"

For your information

 

If the chocolate was eaten recently (withing 1-2hours), the vet may choose to induce vomiting to empty the contents of the stomach.

 

Knowing the size of the dog, helps us determine how serious it is. The larger the dog, the more chocolate they can consume before reaching toxic levels. ​​​​​​​

 

Symptoms of theobromine poisoning can take up to 6-12 hours to develop.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Chocolate Toxicity Calculator (guide only!)

 

Only use this calculator if the client cannot or will not bring their pet straight down. The calculator will help you advise on the seriousness and should not be used to determine if the pet should come down or not.

 

All clients should be advised to bring the patient in immediately. Vets will decide the course of action required after examination.

 

https://petsci.co.uk/tools/chocolate-toxicity-calculator/chocolate-toxicity-calculator.html

{"html":"

DOG ATTACK / FIGHTS


Description

  • Dog fights

Urgency

  • RED: Come straight down

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Procedure

  • Book with any vet - general appointment duration


"}

{"html":"

For your learning

 

Not all bite wounds tear the skin, but they can still cause significant internal crushing damage. Even small punctures can mean significant trauma. It is for this reason that all animals involved in dog attacks/fights need to be seen immediately. 

 

The vet will perform a physical exam on the patient and may need to start life saving interventions immediately if there is significant trauma. Pain relief is administered to the patient alongside antibiotics to prevent infection from bacteria entering the body through wound sites.

Surgery is usually required so the extent of the injuries can be assessed, the wounds debrided and decontaminated and closed if possible to ensure a good recovery for the pet. Sometimes repeat surgeries are required and sometimes drains are placed temporarily to help decontaminate the wound and reduce the ‘dead space’ (space creating by the pet’s jaw shaking the layers apart).

 

If the vet is concerned about internal injuries, imaging such as x-rays and ultrasound maybe performed.

 

Puncture wounds can go as deep as the abdomen and lead to organ damage and internal bleeding. Emergency abdominal surgery may be required to repair the injury.

Puncture wounds can also enter the chest and can extend deep enough to puncture the lungs, leading to bleeding or air leaking into the chest cavity. Emergency open chest surgery may be required to repair these injuries.

 

The vet may also conduct blood tests. In severe dog bite wounds especially involving internal injuries, a blood transfusion may be required.

 

"}

{"html":"

DIFFICULTY BREATHING OR HEATSTROKE🚑


Description

An animal that is struggling to breathe or can't breathe. 

Procedure

EMERGENCY – Come straight down!🚑 Not being able to breathe is not good! 

"}

{"html":"

​​​​​​​Advice to clients 👈

 

IF HEATSTOKE


If their arrival will be delayed (eg waiting for transport, waiting for assistance to lift pet etc), ask the client to do the following:

  • Remove the pet from the hot environment immediately.
  • Apply or spray tepid/cool water onto their fur and skin. Then apply a fan/fanning to maximise heat loss.
  • Wet down the area around the pet (where possible)
  • Don’t use ice-cold water or ice as this may worsen the problem.
  • Get down to the clinic as soon as possible.


"}

{"html":"

Make sure you tell the Hospital Leader than you have an animal coming down that is having trouble breathing. They will prepare the hospital for the patient's arrival.

"}

{"html":"

For your information

 

Potential Causes

 

BOAS: Breeds like French Bulldogs, Boxers, Bulldogs, Boston Terriers, Shih Tzus, Pekinese and Pugs (brachycephalics) have bones in their skull which are shorter in length, giving the ‘flat face’ appearance and a short snout. 

 

Brachycephalic airway syndrome (BOAS) is a difficulty that the above breeds can suffer from, causing their breathing and airways to become abnormal. Dogs PANT to cool down, if they can’t breathe properly they overheat. 

 

Heatstroke: Heatstroke, or heat exhaustion can have a huge impact on a dog’s breathing and respiratory health. Heatstroke can be extremely dangerous and can be fatal.🥵

"}

{"html":"




FOOD TOXICITY🚑  


Description

 

The pet has eaten a food which is toxic to them.

Some of these foods are;

 

  • Chocolate (see one pager on Chocolate Toxicity)
  • Onions

  • Grapes
  • Sultanas
  • Macadamia Nuts​​​​​​​
  •  

Procedure

 

EMERGENCY – Come straight down! 🚑 

 

"}

{"html":"

For your information

 

If the food was eaten recently, the vet may choose to induce vomiting to empty the contents of the stomach.

​​​​​​​IV fluids and other medications may be required. This depends on how much was eaten and the patients size, breed etc. ​​​​​​​

Advice to clients 👈


If the animal is not moving


Approach the animal with caution. An injured, frightened or disoriented dog or cat might bite, even if it's their owner.

RAT BAIT


Description

The pet ate rat bait – a poison designed to kill vermin.

Procedure

EMERGENCY – Come straight down! 🚑

{"html":"

Advice to clients 👈

Ask the client to bring down the rat bait packaging!

"}

{"html":"

For your information

 

Death from Internal Bleeding: 3 - 7 days.

 

​​​​​​​After eating these baits, animals often remain without symptoms for many days before developing potentially life-threatening bleeding. This can provide a false sense of reassurance to the owner that their pet will be OK.

 

If the rat bait was eaten recently, the vet may choose to induce vomiting to empty the contents of the stomach. 

 

Rodenticides act as anticoagulants (prevent the blood from clotting). They deplete the body’s supply of vitamin K, which is essential in the formation of clotting agents in the blood stream. This causes;

 

  1. Internal bleeding
  2. Brain swelling
  3. High calcium levels (which can lead to things like kidney failure).
  4.  

Most domestic rat and mouse baits available in Australia contain anticoagulants which prevent the blood from clotting. The bittering agents which are added to many of the baits, do not seem to prevent dogs from eating them.

"}

{"html":"

SEIZURES  


Description

 

Seizures are caused by a sudden surge of uncontrollable electrical activity within the brain. 

 

Procedure

 

URGENT - but not an emergency

 

  • Come down when the seizure finishes & dog is near normal again.


"}

{"html":"

Advice to clients

If the animal is still seizing? If so.....

 

  • Don’t panic! Most seizures only last for a minute or so and don’t cause any long-term damage. Stay calm!
  • Remove anything from the dog’s surroundings that might injure them (sharp edges, floor lamp, chairs etc) and let the seizure run its course. No need to hold or comfort them, just let them ride it out.
  • If the dog is in a potentially dangerous area eg stairwell, try to gently move them to a safer spot.
  •  

If the seizure is over....


After the seizure is over, keep the dog in a safe area and monitor them until they come out of their post-ictal phase. Once the dog is steady on their feet and are mostly back to normal, bring them down to the practice so we can try and find the cause. If the dog becomes aggressive during this stage, do not approach them. It is temporary and will pass. Stay calm.

Come down immediately if the dog experiences any of the following:

 

A seizure that lasts longer than 5-10 minutes.

Seizures that cluster together and don’t give the dog enough time to recover in between.

More than two seizures in 24 hours.

No food or water! It can make it hard for the dog to breathe!

"}

{"html":"



​​​​​​​General Information

 

Dogs who are having seizures need veterinary attention. Left untreated, seizures tend to get worse, which can lead to permanent neurological damage, or death. 

 

What does a seizure look like?

 

They are completely unaware of their surroundings.

They fall over and become stiff.

They paddle their limbs.

They may urinate or defecate.

 

Post-ictal Stage - After the seizure has ended, dogs will go through a phase called the post-ictal stage. During this stage, they may be lethargic, restless, wobbly on their feet, or even go temporarily blind and bump into walls. They may also bark and become aggressive temporarily. This usually lasts from a few minutes to a few hours. 

"}

{"html":"

Seizures can be terrifying. Try and calm the client as much as possible. If the client calls during the pet's seizure, ask them to take a video.

TICK PARALYSIS 🚑


Description

  • A serious parasite that injects a toxin causing paralysis that can be fatal. Tick paralysis affects both dogs & cats.

Urgency

  • EMERGENCY – Come straight down! 🚑

---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

 

Procedure 

  • Book with any vet - general appointment duration


"}

{"html":"

​​​​​​​Advice to clients 👈


  • If you've removed the tick, please bring it in for identification. You can use a secure ziplock bag, small jar with lid or container with lid. Anything sealed.
  • Do not offer any food or water.


"}

{"html":"

For your learning


General information

 

  • The paralysis tick is a small eight-legged, egg-shaped arachnid, approximately 3-5mm in length. Their appearance varies depending on their life-stage. They are extremely toxic to dogs and cats and can cause death. The paralysis tick is normally a pink colour.
  • Early treatment is a key element to successful recovery from tick paralysis and deterioration can occur in a short space of time, often within hours. ​​​​​​​
  • Even if the client has removed the tick (or several ticks), it is still important that the animal is seen. Pets can continue to worsen for up to three days after a tick has been removed. The poison ticks inject, remains active in the pet’s system for 1-2 weeks after it has been removed.
  •  

Early signs of tick paralysis

  • Lethargy, Reduced appetite, Occasional vomiting.
  •  

Later stages of tick paralysis can include – URGENT

 

  • Wobbly gait (often back legs).
  • Reluctance to move, stand or jump.
  • Change in bark or meow.
  • Cannot blink.
  • Difficulty breathing or rapid breathing.
  • Change in heart rhythm or rate.
  • Excessive drooling.
  • Completely paralysed.


"}

{"html":"

TOAD TOXICITY 🚑


Description

 

  • Cane toad poisoning in dogs occurs when a dog bites or licks a toad. The toad releases a toxin from glands behind the neck and sticks to the gums and tongue of the dog.

Urgency

 

  • EMERGENCY – Come straight down! 🚑

---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

 

Procedure 

 

  • Book with any vet - general appointment duration


"}

{"html":"

Advice to clients 👈

 

​​​​​​​If the dog is seizuring or having tremors 

  • Bring straight down to the clinic
  •  

If the dog has just licked the toad

  • Use a damp cloth, wipe the inside of the dog's mouth to remove the toxin. Rinse the cloth under cool running water after every wipe and keep wiping until the slimy coating has been removed. This can take 10 to 20 minutes. Be cautious as dogs may bite. The toxin sticks to the roof of the dog's mouth so make sure you focus on this area. Never use a hose to flush the toxin from their mouth! This can make them inhale the water causing life-threatening pneumonia. Bring the dog to us immediately after.


"}

{"html":"

For your learning


​​​​​​​Symptoms of toad toxicity in dogs can include:

  • Drooling and foaming at the mouth
  • Change of gum colour. Gums will go \"Brick Red\"
  • Vomiting
  • Diarrhea
  • Loss of coordination or disorientation
  • Rapid or irregular heartbeat
  • Seizures or convulsions
  • Collapse or loss of consciousness
  •  

How does poisoning occur?

  • Poisoning occurs when a dog comes in contact with a cane toad through ‘mouthing’ the toad, biting or licking. When a cane toad is attacked or threatened, they release a potent and fast-acting toxin, milky white in colour, from their parotid glands. They can also squirt the poison up to two metres.
  • The toxin elicits its effects when it is absorbed via the mucous membranes, most commonly the gums but also via the eyes, nose and tongue. It is very rarely ingested. For example, if a cane toad is ‘mouthed’ the toxin will stick to the tongue and gums your pet, which rapidly absorbs across the mucous membranes and into the bloodstream where it targets the heart, gastrointestinal tract, and nervous system.
  •  

​​​​​​​How long does cane toad poisoning take to kill a dog?

  • There is no firm answer to this question, as it depends on how much toxin has been absorbed and the size of the dog. Generally speaking, the adult cane toad has enough toxin to kill an average-sized dog in 15 minutes. The smaller the dog, or cat, the more seriously affected they will be. If your dog does come into contact with the toxin, early intervention is crucial for recovery.

It is not common in cats as they rarely go near the toads.

Procedure - Zydax

 

ZYDAX (arthritis injection) is administered on the same day each week 4 weeks.

  • First injection - Vet Appointment 👩‍⚕️
  • Second injection - Nurse Appointment
  • Third injection - Nurse Appointment
  • Fourth Injection - Vet Appointment 👩‍⚕️

Clients should see a reduction of osteoarthritis signs after 2 or 3 injections.

The initial course of injections typically provides 3 – 6 months of relief from the problems associated with osteoarthritis. Our vets will recommend when another course of 4 injections is due.

Clients typically book for all 4 injections at the initial consultation.

 

Procedure - Beransa for dogs

 

Beransa is adminstered once per month.

  •  First injection - Vet Appointment 👩‍⚕️
  • Injections given every month between 6 monthly vet visits can be with a nurse.

Clients should see the best results from their pet 2 weeks after the 2nd injections (so 6 weeks after starting)

 

Procedure - Beransa for Cats

 

Beransa is adminstered once per month.

  •  First injection - Vet Appointment 👩‍⚕️

Clients should see the best results from their pet 2 weeks after the 2nd injections (so 6 weeks after starting)

For your learning

 

Zydax acts in multiple ways;

  1. Stimulates cartilage producing cells to produce healthy cartilage.
  2. Slows cartilage damage by destructive enzymes.

  4. Reduces swelling and blocks inflammatory processes.
  5. Improves blood flow and nutrition to joint structures.
  6.  

Beransa/Solensia:

  1.  Targets and neutralises the nerve growth factor responsible for pain perception in dogs.
  2. Is not a replacement for Zydax - work in conjunction with
  3. Is not metabolised through kidneys like NSAIDS (metacam etc)

For your learning


  • Ear infections are painful. Many dogs will shake their head and scratch their ears trying to relieve the discomfort.
  • When a dog with uncomfortable ears shakes and scratches vigorously, a blood vessel in the earflap may rupture. This leads to bleeding into the tissue called 'Aural Haematoma'. The client might say the dog has a bubble on their ear like a blown up balloon.
  • Nearly all ear infections that are properly diagnosed and treated, can be successfully managed.
  • Several recheck examinations may be needed before the outcome is successful.
  • Dogs with floppy ears or who have lots of hair, are more susceptible to ear infections.

  • Allergy
  • Bacterial and yeast infections

CONSULT FOR BLOODS (MEDICATION MONITORING)


Description

  • We need to see patients on Chronic long-term medications every 6months
  • Some medications require bloods every 6-12 months to make sure dosing is correct
  • Some medications require bloods more frequently if the patient is new to the medication or unstable. The Vet will advise the client on this time frame. 

Urgency

  • GREEN

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Procedure 

  • Book with Vet who is looking after the Patient however if unavailable any vet will do.
  • See advice to client to know at what time to book consult for. Some conditions need to have Bloods taken at a certain time before or after the medication has been given.
  • If blood collections aren't able to be collected in allocated testing times or opening hours vets prefer to have the patient miss the morning dose and have bloods collected first thing so book an 8am appt. PLEASE CONFIRM WITH VET PRIOR TO GIVING THIS ADVISE TO CLIENT


"}

{"html":"

​​​​​​​Advice to clients 👈

 

Please schedule appointments at the following times: 

  • T4 Levels (Hyperthyroid) 4-6 hours post dosing and ideally fasted for 12hours prior
  • Phenobarbitone (Pheno test)- Fasted for 12hrs and blood taken within 1 hour of the next scheduled dose
  • Cushing's Test (ACTH)  4hours post Trilostane (Vetoryl) Administration
  • ACTH Protocol: 
  • 1. Patient has blood collected. (0hr). 
  • 2. Then given the drug Synacthen. (0hr)
  • 3. Blood is collected again at 1hr post Synacthen administration. 
  • - Patient is able to stay in hospital for this procedure and we can take the bloods at times required. Alternative is Client brings dog in and book an appt with the vet. The client can then take the dog home and bring back in 1hr and a nurse can take the final blood.
  • Addisons - Full Body Function with electrolytes. Book appointment anytime as medication is given by injections ONCE a Month.
  • Longterm/Chronic NSAID (Non Steroidal Anti-inflammatory Drugs ie. Metacam) - Book appt anytime
  • Anxiety Medications (ie. Fluoxetine/Zactin) - Book appointment anytime
  • Other Medication - Check with Vet/Senior Nurse before booking

{"html":"

HEARTWORM INJECTIONS SR12


Description

 

Heartworm is a disease spread by mosquitoes. It affects both dogs and cats but is much more common in dogs. The SR12 injection can only be given to dogs.

Cats should use an over-the-counter heartworm preventative.

 

Procedure

NOT URGENT - next available appointment

---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

 

​​​​​​​Procedure

 

Check the client file first to ensure it is just heartworm due and not a vaccination also!

Vaccinations and Heartworm injections are commonly done together!

HOW TO BOOK

 

  1. Heartworm injection ONLY with no other concerns? Nurse appointment x 10mins
  2. Heartworm injection with one concern to address? Vet appointment x 20mins 👩‍⚕️
  3. Heartworm injection PLUS a Vaccination? Vet appointment x 20mins 👩‍⚕️
  4.  

Protocol

  1. First injection - 12 weeks of age. Prior to this age, monthly protection is advised.
  2. Second injection - 9 months of age.
  3. Yearly booster for life.
  4.  

If given at 6months of age, second injection is given 12 months later. 

Booster Overdue? If the booster is 3 months or more OVERDUE, a Heartworm Test will be required in 3 months to ensure the dog did not contract heartworm during the time it was unprotected. It is still safe to administer the SR12 injection, even if the pet is overdue.

 

You do not need to discuss this with the client. Our vets will discuss this with the client during consult. Just flag it is overdue more than 3 months. If it's overdue but LESS than 3 months write 'NO' to overdue as the patient will not need a Heartworm Test.

{"html":"

When do female dogs have their first heat cycle?

 

From 6 months of age (usually at 9 or 10 months), and even later in large and giant breeds (up to 24 months).

 

 What are the signs?

 

Most notable sign is vaginal bleeding. This may not become apparent until a few days after the female has actually come into oestrus. Vulvar swelling should be taken as the first sign in addition to the female paying increased attention (such as licking the area) to her rear end.

 

From the beginning of the heat period she will be attractive to male dogs, but will usually not be receptive, or allow mating, until about 7-10 days later. Discharge will usually become less bloodstained.

 

 How often does a female come into heat?

 

They cycle about every 6 to 8 months, although this can be extremely variable.

 

 How long does it last?

 

The first sign of heat is vaginal bleeding which lasts for 9 to 14 days, and ends when the bitch allows mating. Standing heat or oestrus lasts another 9 days or so.

 

 When is the best time for mating?

 

The first few days of oestrus are considered to be the most fertile time of the cycle, so mating at this time is more likely to be successful. Vaginal discharge is still present and classically attains a straw colour at this point.

 

 How long does pregnancy last?

 

58-68 days (approx. 9 weeks)

 

 Pregnancy Signs For Dogs

 

Noticeable signs of pregnancy for a dog can vary from canine to canine. They may have all or some of the following signs/symptoms if pregnant:

 

  • Weight gain
  • Swollen abdomen
  • Enlarged nipples
  • An increased appetite
  • Increased tiredness or unwillingness to play
  • Changes in mood, often becoming irritable or affectionate

{"html":"

Oestrous Cycles in Cats (Heat Cycle)

 

When does a female cat have her first oestrus cycle?

 

Cats have their first estrous (reproductive) cycle when they reach puberty – approx. 6 months.

 

How often does a female cat come into heat?

 

Cats are seasonally polyestrous, which means that they have multiple cycles during the breeding season. The breeding season will vary according to geography and environmental factors such as temperature and the number of daylight hours.

 

How long does oestrus last?

 

Average length being seven days. If the queen (an intact female cat) is not mated during oestrus, she will go out of heat for a short period of time, usually about seven days. Therefore, the complete estrous cycle of a cat can range from anywhere between one to six weeks, with the average cycle length being about three weeks.

 

What are the signs of oestrus?

 

The most notable signs of oestrus in cats are behavioral. Most cats become very affectionate, even demanding; they persistently rub against their owners (or objects such as furniture), constantly wanting attention. They roll on the floor more often.

\"The most notable signs of oestrus in cats are behavioural.\"

 

At what stage of the estrous cycle is the cat able to get pregnant?

 

The queen can be bred at any time while in heat. Cats are induced ovulators, which means that the act of breeding stimulates the release of eggs from the ovaries.

 

Most females require three to four matings within a 24-hour period for ovulation to occur. It only takes a minute or two for cats to mate, and cats may mate multiple times in a short period of time. Queens may mate with several different tomcats during this time, so it is possible that a litter of kittens may have several different fathers. Once ovulation has occurred, the queen will go out of heat within a day or two.

 

How long does pregnancy last in a cat?

 

Approximately 64 to 71 days with an average of 65 days (nine weeks).

We prioritise the care of sick animals, and it's the responsibility of the council to manage strays. Compromising sick patients in our care with stray animals, will never align with our standard of care. 




The fastest way to return strays to their owners is through;

The Gold Coast City Council (finders home or holding pens)

The Facebook Page - ‘Gold Coast Lost and Found’


We are unable to take in stray dogs unless; 

 

  1. The stray has identification
  2. We can speak directly to the owner
  3. The owner can collect within 2 hours
  4.  

The council does not guarantee same-day collection of stray dogs from our practice, and they do not provide any collection service on weekends. However, they guarantee collection from a private residence within two hours, or the same day from Council holding pens. 

Note: The finder does not have to pay any fees.

Our hospital has multiple surgeries scheduled each day, and maintaining a stress-free, quiet environment is crucial for our patients' recovery. A barking stray dog in the hospital could jeopardise this.


Procedure


Tell the client you cannot take the dog for the above reasons (won't be collected, negative impact on patients), but you are happy to scan the animal for a microchip while they wait.

  • Scan animal
  • Look up Pet Address to get owners details. 
  • Search our database (RX) to see if it is a patient of ours.
  • Take name and best contact number of person who found the dog incase the owner contact us.
  • Put animals details with finders info into the “Found” clipboard in your clinics RX works sidebar.
  •  

Chipped & a VL Client?

If the stray dog is a TVL client, please follow these steps:

1. Accept the dog from the finder, as we are confident we can rehome the dog the same day (a $40 rehoming/housing fee applies).

2. Request the owner to collect the dog within two hours to avoid causing stress to our hospitalised patients.

 

Chipped but NOT a VL Client?

If the stray dog is not a TVL client, follow these steps:

 

1. Attempt to contact the owner direct using the details provided by the microchip company.

2. If you reach the owner and they can collect the dog within two hours, we can take the dog. If not, we cannot accept the dog. The owner can collect the dog from the council (and pay the council fees), or collect from the finders residence (if they approve). 

3. Inform the owner that there will be a $40 housing fee payable upon collection.

 

Can't contact owner? 

Give information sheet to finder ‘What to do if you find a stray animal’ . It lists all addresses & contact numbers of where to go. 


Finder has 4 choices.

1. Take the stray home & call council for collection &/or place a notice on the Facebook Lost and Found page.

2. Take the dog to the GC Council or AWL.

3. Take the dog to a holding pen.

4. Visit another vet to see if its their patient (through chip number).

 

NOTES

 

  1. NSW Pets: Pet Address does not show details of animals microchipped with the NSW Companion Animal Registry. There is no search option for animals microchipped with NSW Council.
  2. Inured animals: If the animal is injured, admit to the hospital for first aid. Call the RSPCA for collection on 1300 264 625.
  3. Wildlife: We accept injured Wildlife.
